---
title: Buoyancy flow (2D)
---

A warm plume rises in a closed square. Its scalar field creates upward
buoyancy, and the resulting incompressible flow transports that scalar.
All backends use no-slip velocity walls and zero normal scalar derivative.

| Backend | Coupled flow implementation | Differentiable inputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PhiFlow | Semi-Lagrangian transport, explicit diffusion, and pressure projection. | State and physics parameters |
| WaterLily | Native momentum and pressure routines, with conservative upwind scalar transport and two-stage coupling added by the adapter. | State and physics parameters |
| Oceananigans | Native nonhydrostatic buoyancy model, third-order upwind advection, RK3, and spectral pressure projection. | State |

The Julia backends initially run on CPU. Each backend generates its own
fine-resolution reference; the physical problem and training recipe are shared,
but the numerical discretizations differ.

Both Julia adapters use Enzyme reverse-mode differentiation. Oceananigans uses
an equivalent separable Neumann pressure inverse because its native FFTW path
lacks Enzyme support. Forward simulation and derivatives use the same pressure
implementation. Its adapter pins Julia 1.12.6 to avoid the reverse-mode
compilation crash observed with Julia 1.11.7 in the Python–Julia runtime.

The benchmark trains a small convolutional neural network to correct velocity
after each solver interval. A streamfunction makes these corrections
divergence-free with zero normal wall velocity. The scalar remains solver-driven.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S[Velocity and scalar] --> P[Coupled solver step]
    P --> N[Neural velocity correction]
    N --> S
    N --> L[Compare with restricted fine reference]
    L -. Training gradient through the rollout .-> N
```

All training methods use the same network initialization, optimizer budget,
training data and validation cases. Fixed-pair supervision uses one-step
targets; solver-in-the-loop training uses a recurrent trajectory loss; the
stopped-gradient ablation uses the same recurrent loss with solver derivatives
removed. Held-out rollouts report velocity and scalar errors separately.

References come from the same solver at finer spatial and temporal resolution.
The experiment checks reference time refinement, restart equivalence, and
end-to-end finite differences before reporting training results. CI checks
correct execution; it does not require a statistical advantage from a short run.

This setup is inspired by [Um et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00016).
It is a bounded benchmark, not a reproduction of their full training campaign.
Results and full-field plots appear here when benchmark artifacts are generated.

```bash
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s phiflow
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s waterlily
mosaic run -p buoyancy-grid --suites forward,gradient,cost,optimization -s oceananigans
```
